background.definition: Benign ovarian tumors are defined as cystic, solid, or semisolid; unilateral; mobile; and smooth noncancerous lesion within the ovary or on the surface of the ovary. These tumors may be functional or nonfunctional. Common types of benign ovarian tumors include: (1) follicular cysts, (2) lutein cysts, (3) mucinous and serous cystadenomas, (4) Brenner tumors, (5) germ cell tumors, and (6) stromal cell tumors. The most common stromal cell tumor is the fibroma. Fibromas are common in Meigs syndrome and Gorlin syndrome. This chapter will address solid tumors.

list.listitem: Incidence of benign ovarian tumors is 18.6/100,000 women per year.
Incidence of benign ovarian tumors in pregnancy is 1 in 112.
250 per 1000 women have fibromas.
Fibromas are found in 2% to 5% of women who undergo surgery for ovarian mass.
Occur in 30% of women with regular menses and 50% of women with irregular menses.
Seventy-five percent of serous tumors and 80% of mucinous ovarian tumors are benign or borderline malignant.
Twenty-five percent of benign serous ovarian tumors are bilateral.
Risk factors are listed below.
Unknown.
Benign ovarian tumors can be components of genetic syndromes, and karyotypic analysis of ovarian stromal tumors suggests abnormalities of chromosomes 4 and 9.
Benign ovarian masses arise during ovulation. These are usually cystic lesions. Most will resolve.
In general, benign ovarian masses tend to decrease as gestational age progresses through spontaneous resolution.
Sixty percent to 70% of ovarian tumors are epithelial in origin, including benign tumors.
The pathophysiology of fibromas is unknown. Ovarian fibromas arise from the stromal tissue of the ovarian cortex.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force does not recommend routine screening for ovarian tumors. A very large RCT with over 75,000 women age 55 to 74 years found no mortality benefit to a program of screening with CA-125 and ultrasound. B

The recent UKCTOCS trial used a special algorithm that incorporated risk factors with CA-125, and found a marginally significant disease specific mortality reduction after 13 years. Additional follow-up is needed to confirm this result.
Encourage smoking cessation; women who smoke cigarettes have a 2- to 5-fold greater risk of developing benign mucinous ovarian tumor. B
Maintaining a body mass index of less than 30 may decrease the risk of serous and mucinous cystadenoma. B
Initial evaluation is with transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound or MRI. C
Gray scale trnsvaginal ultrasound is the preferred method for evaluating the adnexal mass.
Obtain CA-125 in conjunction with imaging studies when the mass is larger than 5 cm or persistence suggests malignancy; this test is suggested for postmenopausal women presenting with adnexal mass. B
Use O-RADS US and MRI categories to classify patients as to likelilhood of malignancy. B
Lesions that increase in size on follow-up or change in character require laparoscopy or surgical exploration for further evaluation. C

May be associated with GI symptoms, pain during ovulation or menses, irregular menses
Lower abdominal pain, adnexal mass, fever, unilateral or bilateral
Postmenopausal woman with adnexal mass, abnormal uterine bleeding, thickened endometrium

list.listitem: Benign ovarian tumors are usually asymptomatic except when there is adnexal torsion, rupture, endometriosis, or the mass enlarges; multiple symptoms (eg, pelvic or abdominal pain, increased abdominal size, fatigue) are more suggestive of malignancy.
Tumors may grow, leading to abdominal distension and compression symptoms.

An enlarged mass may be palpated on bimanual examination. Mobile lesions are more likely benign compared with fixed ovarian solid lesions. Bimanual examination is relatively insensitive but quite specific, meaning that it is helpful when abnormal (LR+ 4.5) but a normal examination does not rule out adnexal mass.

For more information on using the history and physical examination to assess the risk of ovarian cancer; see that chapter. A systematic review concluded that symptoms that significantly increase the risk of ovarian cancer include abdominal mass (LR+ 30), abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16), pelvic pain (LR 10), bloating (LR+ 9), loss of appetite (LR 9) and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5).

Ultrasound is reliable in evaluating whether adnexal masses are cystic or solid, irregular, smooth or septated. Ultrasound findings of a smooth cystic mass with few septae usually indicate a benign lesion. Unilocular cysts are more likely benign compared with multilocular cysts. Increased overgrowth of the epithelial lining of cysts is consistent with malignancy.

The O-RADS US system has been prospectively validated in 227 women with 262 adnexal lesions (AUC 0.91). Rates of malignancy were:
O-RADS US 2: 0/100 (0%) O-RADS US 3: 1/32 (3%) O-RADS US 4: 22/63 (35%) O-RADS US 5: 52/67 (78%)
A large trial of cancer screening found no association between single or multiple ovarian inclusion cysts (anechoic ovarian cysts up to 10 mm in diameter) and cancer.
In a menarchal female with a mass larger than 5 cm, laparoscopy is recommended (see ).
Biopsy with histologic examination is necessary to determine whether the mass is benign or malignant.

Cancer antigen (CA-125) is not helpful in the routine diagnosis of a benign ovarian tumor. However, it is recommended in conjunction with imaging or further evaluation when the mass is larger than 5 cm or if it persists or changes. It is also recommended as part of the evaluation for any postmenopausal woman presenting with adnexal mass.

Other diagnostic tests include: pregnancy tests (woman of reproductive age with missed period or abnormal uterine bleeding), endometrial biopsy (postmenopausal woman with abnormal uterine bleeding), and serum tumor markers as indicated (eg, CA-125 when the mass is larger than 5 cm or persistence suggests malignancy).

A study of 200 women scheduled to have surgery for a pelvic mass used an algorithm consisting of 8 genes and 4 serum biomarkers. It was over 99% sensitive with AUC of 0.95 for identification of stage III - IV ovarian cancers. If validated it may be helpful for prioritizing women who need surgical biopsy.

See chapter on ovarian cancer for more information on the accuracy of ultrasound, CT, MRI, CA-125, and PET scans. MRI is moderately accurate at distinguishing malignant ovarian lesions from non-malignant.
MRI

The O-RADS MRI classification scheme has been shown to have good accuracy with 92% sensitivity and 91% specificity in a meta-analysis of 4012 women (LR+ 10, LR-0.09). The following rates of malignancy by category:
O-RADS MRI cat 2: 0.1% O-RADS MRI cat 3: 6% O-RADS MRI cat 4: 60% O-RADS MRI cat 5: 96%
Most benign ovarian lesions are recognized incidentally on clinical examination or imaging studies.
Initial evaluation should be with transvaginal ultrasound. MRI is useful if cystic teratomas (dermoids) are suspected.
Lesions that increase in size on follow-up or that change in character require laparoscopy or surgical exploration for further evaluation.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Observation is the mainstay for most benign lesions. C
Changing masses, indeterminant masses, or masses suspicious for malignancy require additional evaluation including laparoscopy or surgical exploration with biopsy. C

Laparoscopy compared with laparotomy for suspected benign ovarian tumors is associated with fewer urinary tract infections, postoperative complications, less postoperative pain, and reduced number of days in hospital and total cost. B
Observation is the mainstay for most benign lesions.
Changing masses, indeterminant masses, or masses suspicious for malignancy require additional evaluation.

Some studies suggest that laparoscopy has benefits over laparotomy for patients with suspected benign ovarian tumor, with fewer adverse outcomes such as decreased febrile morbidity, fewer postoperative complications, better pain scores, and decreased total hospital stay and cost. A Cochrane review found no studies comparing laparoscopy versus laparotomy for FIGO stage I ovarian cancer, though.
The decision to proceed with laparotomy must be considered when extra-ovarian lesions or peritoneal involvement is a concern.
Complications of benign ovarian lesions include hemorrhage, rupture of lesion, torsion, and pseudomyxoma peritonei.

A suspicion of ovarian torsion (ie, severe, acute abdominal, or pelvic pain) is an indication for surgical evaluation. A twisted pedicle on ultrasound implies ovarian torsion. However, a high index of suspicion alone should prompt referral for surgical exploration. Hemorrhage during torsion may require aggressive fluid resuscitation to prevent shock.

When a benign lesion such as a dermoid undergoes torsion, conservation of the ovary is preferable if there is no evidence of thromboembolism, ischemia, necrosis, or postoperative infectious morbidity. Laparoscopy is the procedure of choice.

Pseudomyxoma peritonei (the presence in the peritoneal cavity of mucoid matter from a ruptured ovarian cyst or mucocele of the appendix) presents with nonspecific symptoms such as increased abdominal size, pelvic pain, infertility, navel bulging, infertility, and changes in bowel habits. Treatment is variable but may include surgery and removal of tumor and/or mucous. This diagnosis may require more extensive surgery. With pseudomyxoma, preservation of the ovary requires early recognition and diagnosis.
Prognosis is good, with total recovery post resection of benign ovarian mass.
Current evidence does not support malignant transformation in most benign ovarian tumors. However, postmenopausal women with complex ovarian cysts have a 3% risk of malignant transformation. B
A mutation in BRCA1 or BRCA2 is associated with a significantly improved prognosis for women with ovarian cancer. It appears that BRCA2 carriers have the best overall prognosis.
Squamous cell carcinomas can arise from mature cystic teratomas, although this is rare (17 cases over 22 years in one study). B
Repeat ultrasound is recommended in approximately 6 weeks. If an ovarian lesion changes characteristics in texture or size, biopsy is recommended. B

A large observational study (the Nurses's Health Study) found that women had oophorectomy at the time of hysterectomy for reasons other than cancer had an increase in all-cause mortality. This was not a randomized trials, but the effect was substantial (HR 1.13; 95% CI, 1.06-21) despite a decrease in ovarian cancer mortality (HR 0.06; 95% CI, 0.02-0.17). Rates of death due to CHD, lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and total cancers were increased even after adjustment for risk factors.
A palpable adnexal mass, ascites, elevated CA-125, and/or family history of BRCA gene mutations in a postmenopausal woman is highly suspicious for ovarian cancer.
Only 2% to 4% of masses identified in pregnancy are malignant; most are benign and do not affect the mother or fetus.
The two most common cysts in pregnancy are cystadenomas and dermoid.
Solid ovarian tumors during pregnancy are usually benign. These tumors are usually thecomas or fibromas; less than 1% are malignant.

Management depends on the risk for torsion and complications. Initial treatment includes observation with sonographic follow-up. One in 200 masses results in torsion, infarction, or difficulty with vaginal delivery.

Laparoscopy can be performed between 16 and 18 weeks of gestation if a cyst persists after the first trimester or if the lesion needs further evaluation. A Cochrane review identified only case series that provided limited information on the balance of benefits and harms for this procedure in pregnant women.
Benign cystic teratoma is sometimes seen in childhood. Most are treated with cystectomy, leaving the ovary to maintain fertility.

In a case series of ovarian masses diagnosed in children over a 10-year period, the mean age of the 49 children was 13.3 and abdominal pain was the most common presentation. Most benign tumors were teratomas and 8 masses (16%) were malignant (malignant teratoma, dysgerminoma, and germ cell tumors). There were no deaths after a follow-up of 6 years.
